text.title: Interview Recording Redaction Pipeline Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for interview-recording-redaction-pipeline. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Every recording MUST have a consent record (signed or recorded verbal) linked to the file; consent missing → auto-delete after grace period.
rule.rationale: The burden of demonstrating that consent was given sits with whoever holds the recording, so consent that survives only as someone's recollection of a verbal "sure" is indistinguishable from no consent once a subject objects. Linking the record to the specific file is what makes withdrawal actionable, because a withdrawal cannot be honoured against an artefact you cannot identify. Auto-deleting after a grace period converts an unprovable holding into no holding, which is the only defensible end state.

rule.statement: Transcript MUST be generated by a tool the BA controls (local Whisper, on-prem ASR); external SaaS transcript without BAA / DPA is forbidden.
rule.rationale: Uploading a recording to a transcription service is a disclosure: that vendor becomes a processor of the interviewee's data. Without a processing agreement in place there is no contractual limit on how long it retains the audio, which sub-processors it passes it to, or whether the content feeds model training, and the vendor's retention schedule quietly outlives the one the subject was promised. The liability stays with whoever gave that promise, not with the tool that was convenient.

rule.statement: Pipeline MUST auto-redact at least 8 PII categories: names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, SSN/NIE/IPN, credit-card numbers, IP addresses, medical IDs. Output flags un-redactable spans for human review.
rule.rationale: Re-identification rarely needs a name: a job title, an employer, a postcode and a date narrow a transcript to one person, which is why de-identification schemes enumerate identifier categories instead of trusting a reviewer's sense of what looks personal. Enumerating them also makes coverage testable rather than a matter of opinion. Flagging the spans the redactor could not resolve matters as much as the redactions themselves, because a clean-looking output with a silent miss gets trusted and forwarded, while a flagged one gets read.

rule.statement: Auto-redacted transcript MUST pass a named human reviewer before sharing; the review event is logged with reviewer id + timestamp.
rule.rationale: Automated redaction fails precisely where the stakes are highest: indirect references, nicknames, and details that identify someone only in combination. The second pair of eyes exists to catch what a pattern matcher structurally cannot see. Recording the reviewer's identity and the timestamp is what stops the checkpoint decaying into a rubber stamp, because an unattributed review leaves nobody owning the miss when it surfaces.

rule.statement: Retention tiered: raw recording 30 days, redacted transcript 12 months, derived analysis 5 years; each tier auto-deletes after its window.
rule.rationale: A single window across all three artefacts forces a bad trade: short enough for raw audio destroys the analysis, long enough for the analysis leaves the highest-risk artefact in storage for years after the only reason to keep it expired. Tiering lets each window track the risk and the actual purpose of that artefact rather than the longest need in the chain. Deletion has to be automatic because manual clean-up is the task that never reaches the top of anyone's list.

rule.statement: Every access to raw recording or unredacted transcript MUST be logged (who, when, why); access without logging is treated as a breach.
rule.rationale: After an incident the only answerable question is who actually saw what, and with no log the exposure cannot be bounded, so every subject in the archive has to be treated as affected instead of the handful who really were. Classifying unlogged access as a breach in its own right is what removes the incentive to reach around the logging path when it is inconvenient; otherwise the log captures only the well-behaved accesses and is worthless as evidence.

rule.statement: If a recording leaks (storage breach, access without log, redaction failure), engage breach process: notify within 24h, isolate, root-cause within 7 days.
rule.rationale: The regulatory clock starts when the organisation becomes aware of the breach, not when it finishes investigating, so an undefined process burns the window arguing about who has authority to call it a breach at all. An internal deadline set well inside the external one is what leaves time to notify with facts rather than a placeholder. Isolation comes first because an unisolated leak keeps widening while paperwork is drafted, and the root-cause deadline exists because an incident closed without one recurs through the same mechanism.

rule.statement: If no recordings exist or BA has no custody of recordings, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Every rule here attaches to custody of an artefact. Where the BA never holds a recording there is nothing for the pipeline to act on, and standing one up anyway tends to produce a second copy of data the BA was not supposed to hold, raising exposure instead of lowering it. In that case the control belongs to whoever does have custody, and duplicating it locally weakens theirs.
